sampling: stratified and balanced (10K per type); authors: with a balanced test set the metrics are 'not directly applicable' to real distributions
tools evaluated and headline results: Magika 99% average F1 (binary 100%, text 99%). Baselines on the text types each tool supports: guesslang 77% (29 of 113 types), exiftool 70%, file --mime 68%, trid 68%, file 67% (one note gives file 68%); on all 43 text types: guesslang 52%, file 48%, file --mime 42%, trid 35%, exiftool 22%. Per-type cells of Table III are marked [check] in the notes, including anomalous '100' cells for exiftool and trid on JAVASCRIPT and for file --mime, exiftool and trid on POWERSHELL. Examples: guesslang C 91%, Python 90%, HTML 60%, XML 31%. Linguist, go-enry, Pygments and cloc are not compared; no LLM

tools evaluated and headline results: none; a blog analysis (Derek Jones, grey literature) reports 2,836,119 unique suffixes and criticises the suffix filter
availability and licence: derived datasets on Software Heritage S3; code archived by SWHID
known issues: one name per content; ambiguous extensions resolved by hand; the paper anticipates rebuilding 'When Software Heritage will provide information on the programming language for each of its file contents'
relevance to us: high — the natural sampling frame for a population-sampled benchmark over Software Heritage, and the baseline labelling that Synid would replace

name / short id: E12 World of Code (WoC) language field
reference: Ma et al., "World of Code: enabling a research workflow for mining and analyzing the universe of open source VCS data", arXiv:2010.16196 <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.16196> (Empirical Software Engineering 2021 and author list from memory, unverified); rule set read in woc.pm <https://github.com/ssc-oscar/lookup/blob/aebe8f0d1925855fca02e2dc2bd60f077ce48e51/woc.pm>
size: 7.9 B blobs, 12.4 B files, 123.8 M projects (March 2020); 35 language buckets
label source and quality: 35 regular expressions on the file name, 'Unknown' otherwise; .h under C, .m under ObjectiveC, .rst under Rust, .json under JS; older maps also carry a language 'as determined by ctags'; no validation published
taxonomy: own coarse buckets, including families such as 'Fml'
splits and leakage control: not applicable; blobs are content-addressed; projects deforked
tools evaluated and headline results: none. Source comments record ctags-vs-extension counts ('92842;m;MatLab vs 180971;m;ObjectiveC'), an informal sign that about one third of the counted .m files were MATLAB
availability and licence: access conditions not captured (worldofcode.org unreachable in this review)
known issues: noisy and coarse rules; for names matched by two regexes the label can depend on hash order (a researcher's reading of the code)
relevance to us: low — usable as a sampling frame, not as labels

name / short id: E13 Boa file kinds
reference: boalang/compiler: AbstractCommit.java <https://github.com/boalang/compiler/blob/4e5c5383b39afc244634d3256a99e357716229a4/src/java/boa/datagen/scm/AbstractCommit.java> and diff.proto <https://github.com/boalang/compiler/blob/4e5c5383b39afc244634d3256a99e357716229a4/src/proto/diff.proto>. Paper (Dyer, Nguyen, Rajan, Nguyen, ICSE 2013) from memory, unverified
size: not captured
label source and quality: extension dispatch followed by parser acceptance: e.g. .java starts as SOURCE_JAVA_ERROR and is upgraded to a JLS level when a parse succeeds
taxonomy: Java, JavaScript, PHP, HTML, XML, CSS with language levels
tools evaluated and headline results: none; the share of parse-error kinds among .java files would estimate extension-label error, but no publication reporting it was found
availability and licence: infrastructure public (site unreachable in this review)
known issues: few languages
relevance to us: low — a design precedent: record whether the extension-implied parser accepts the file

name / short id: E14 GitHub repository-level language metadata (GHTorrent, Libraries.io, GitHub Innovation Graph, 'gha_language')
reference: GHTorrent relational schema <https://github.com/ghtorrent/ghtorrent.org/blob/51890965af72da85bdd0954a50ef1a71603fb4e7/relational.md> (Gousios, MSR 2013, from memory); Libraries.io repository.rb <https://github.com/librariesio/libraries.io/blob/fbc438e24ca24f1615d4baa00037d32d688d0677/app/models/repository.rb>; GitHub Innovation Graph datasheet <https://github.com/github/innovationgraph/blob/078fb62ee4395d321bec9f4f06694cca68f6b6cb/docs/datasheet.md> (CC0, v1.0.11 of 2026-07-07)
size: Innovation Graph languages.csv: 180,338 rows, 404 language names, 2020 Q1 to 2026 Q1 (own count)
label source and quality: GitHub's primary language and per-language byte counts, i.e. Linguist after excluding vendored, generated, documentation, data and prose files; Libraries.io pins Linguist 7.4.0
"not code" / "other" labels?: Innovation Graph has a 'language_type' column (programming, markup, data, prose)
sampling: all public repositories (Innovation Graph: developers pushing per economy and quarter)
tools evaluated and headline results: none
availability and licence: Innovation Graph public (CC0); GHTorrent probably discontinued (from memory)
known issues: a repository's primary language is not a per-file label; several PLI sets nevertheless use it as one (A02, A04, A07, B04)
relevance to us: low — explains where repository-level labels come from; the only openly documented GitHub-side population statistic

name / short id: E15 GitHub public dataset on Google BigQuery (github_repos)
reference: Google Open Source blog, June 2016 <https://opensource.googleblog.com/2016/06/github-on-bigquery-analyze-all-code.html>. Grey literature; schema details from memory (unverified)
size: 'more than 2.8 million open source GitHub repositories', 'almost 2 billion files'
file source: GitHub repositories with an open-source licence
label source and quality: repository-level language bytes (schema unverified); file-level language is not provided, users derive it from the extension
"not code" / "other" labels?: contents table holds non-binary files under 1 MB
tools evaluated and headline results: none
known issues: source of extension-labelled corpora such as codeparrot/github-code and the Verilog corpus of Thakur et al.
relevance to us: low — upstream of several extension-labelled corpora

name / short id: E16 Debsources language statistics
reference: Debian/debsources plugins hook_sloccount.py <https://github.com/Debian/debsources/blob/da6da5c1d725ca88d60594a5bfa8d712e0303737/lib/debsources/plugins/hook_sloccount.py> and hook_ctags.py <https://github.com/Debian/debsources/blob/da6da5c1d725ca88d60594a5bfa8d712e0303737/lib/debsources/plugins/hook_ctags.py>. Papers (Zacchiroli, ESEM 2014; EMSE) from memory, unverified
size: not captured; 34 language names in the vocabulary file read (own count)
label source and quality: sloccount per package and (exuberant) ctags per symbol
tools evaluated and headline results: none
known issues: no validation
relevance to us: low — a non-GitHub population with tool-derived labels

name / short id: E17 Ray et al. 2014 GitHub dataset and its reproduction by Berger et al. 2019
reference: Ray, Posnett, Filkov, Devanbu, "A Large Scale Study of Programming Languages and Code Quality in GitHub", FSE 2014 (DOI from memory, unverified); Berger, Hollenbeck, Maj, Vitek, Vitek, "On the Impact of Programming Languages on Code Quality: A Reproduction Study", ACM TOPLAS 2019, DOI 10.1145/3340571 (volume and article number from memory), arXiv:1901.10220 <https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.10220>
size: 729 projects, 17 languages, 1.58 M commits
file names available?: commits attributed by the extension of the files touched
label source and quality: project language from Linguist; commit language from file extension. Audit by Berger et al.: of 41 projects labelled TypeScript 'only 16 contained TypeScript', because .ts 'is used for XML files containing human language translations' and the Linguist of the time misclassified them (fixed 6 December 2014 per the paper); only .cpp counted as C++; no .h commits
"not code" / "other" labels?: CSS, Shell and Vim script disregarded as not general-purpose
tools evaluated and headline results: none (label audit, at project level)
known issues: a polysemous-extension label error that changed a published conclusion; it reflects a 2014 Linguist bug and must not be quoted as Linguist's current error rate
relevance to us: medium — the best-documented cost of unaudited extension and Linguist labels

name / short id: E18 PolyCoder corpus
reference: Xu, Alon, Neubig, Hellendoorn, arXiv:2202.13169 <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.13169> (title not captured in the notes)
size: 24.1 M files (254 GB) after deduplication; 12 languages
file source: most popular GitHub repositories with at least 50 stars, cloned October 2021
label source and quality: repository majority language propagated to 'each file belonging to the majority-language of that project' (how per file is not stated)
splits and leakage control: not a benchmark; exact-hash deduplication removed nearly 30% of files
sampling: star threshold, about 25K repositories per language
tools evaluated and headline results: none
known issues: repository label used as file label
relevance to us: low — contrast case

name / short id: E19 Jupyter notebooks on GitHub (Källén et al.)
reference: Källén, Sigvardsson, Wrigstad, "Jupyter Notebooks on GitHub: Characteristics and Code Clones", Programming 2021, arXiv:2007.10146 <https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.10146>
size: 2,739,464 notebooks
label source and quality: notebook metadata, four fields in priority order; 2,083 notebooks (0.077%) had conflicting declarations; 2.19% unknown
taxonomy: kernel languages: Python 95.35%, Julia 0.82%, R 0.79%, Scala 0.19%
tools evaluated and headline results: none; cell magics (%%bash, %%R, SQL) not analysed
known issues: composite files with one declared language
relevance to us: low — an example of a container format where the label is a declaration

name / short id: E20 X-COBOL and XMainframe (rare-language corpora)
reference: Ali, Manjunath, Chimalakonda, X-COBOL, arXiv:2306.04892 <https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.04892>, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7968845; Dau et al., XMainframe, arXiv:2408.04660 <https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04660>
size: X-COBOL: 84 repositories, 1,255 COBOL files; XMainframe: 33,561 files after filtering
label source and quality: how files were identified as COBOL is not stated in the abstract
tools evaluated and headline results: none
known issues: XMainframe: 'The amount of COBOL code available on the Internet is much smaller compared to other languages'
relevance to us: low — possible seed material for a legacy-language stratum

name / short id: F01 Govdocs1
reference: Garfinkel, Farrell, Roussev, Dinolt, "Bringing Science to Digital Forensics with Standardized Forensic Corpora", DFRWS 2009 (DOI not retrieved). Corpus page: digitalcorpora.org <https://digitalcorpora.org/corpora/files/>; downloads at https://downloads.digitalcorpora.org/corpora/files/govdocs1/ (not fetched)
size: 'nearly 1 million' files; 986,278 after removals; 63 file types per one downstream paper, with 20 types making up 99.3% (secondary)
label source and quality: file extension only; the corpus page warns it is suggestive and not guaranteed; FiFTy found RTF and TXT 'very often structured and mislabeled'
"not code" / "other" labels?: txt, log, csv and similar text classes; no unknown class
taxonomy: file extensions; almost no programming languages (.java present with 2 samples in three folders, per one paper)
sampling: random web searches by file type; strongly imbalanced
tools evaluated and headline results: dozens of fragment classifiers; e.g. a semi-supervised GAN on byte histograms of 2,946 whole files, 11 classes: 97.55% (XML worst at 83%, confused with HTML); SIFT on 512-byte fragments, 20 classes incl. 'UNK': true-positive rate 80%
availability and licence: free redistribution; per-file metadata server reported unavailable
known issues: old; label noise acknowledged; contains real malware; office formats under-represented (NapierOne authors)
relevance to us: low — a negative control: what happens when a standard corpus is labelled by extension

name / short id: F02 FILETYPES1 (Sceadan training samples)
reference: Beebe, "FILETYPES1 File type samples", University of Texas at San Antonio, 2014: digitalcorpora announcement <https://digitalcorpora.org/2014/02/05/announcing-new-file-type-sample-files/>. Tool paper: Beebe, Maddox, Liu, Sun, "Sceadan", IEEE TIFS 8(9):1519-1530, 2013 (verified via an index)
size: 32 types; file counts not stated on the page
file source: downloaded files, listed in a README with copyright statements
label source and quality: file type of the collected sample
tools evaluated and headline results: Sceadan (SVM on unigrams and bigrams): '73.4% classification rate across 38 file and data types' in the abstract; 73.8% in FiFTy's table (sources disagree)
known issues: evaluation set composition not read from the primary paper
relevance to us: low — one of two forensic corpora with script classes

name / short id: F03 FFT-75 (FiFTy)
reference: Mittal, Korus, Memon, "FiFTy: Large-scale File Fragment Type Identification using Convolutional Neural Networks", IEEE TIFS vol. 16, pp. 28-41 (volume and pages secondary), arXiv:1908.06148, read at ar5iv <https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1908.06148>. Dataset: IEEE DataPort, DOI 10.21227/kfxw-8084 <https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/file-fragment-type-fft-75-dataset> (alive)
size: 75 types x 102,400 blocks, about 7.68 M blocks per block size; about 50.67 GB
file source: 'public files from various public Internet sources and from our own collection'
label source and quality: file type of the source file, inherited by every block
"not code" / "other" labels?: nine human-readable types (TXT, MD, RTF, TEX, LOG, HTML, CSV, JSON, XML as extracted, to check); no programming languages; no unknown class
taxonomy: 75 types in 11 groups; six scenarios at different granularities
splits and leakage control: blocks shuffled into 80/10/10; no statement that blocks of one source file stay in one split; source files not distributed
tools evaluated and headline results: scenario 1, 4,096-byte blocks: FiFTy 77.5%, Sceadan 69.0%; later models 78% to 84% (ByteRCNN 83.9%; several of these figures are secondary); on a Govdocs1 subset FiFTy drops to 55.9% (to check the exact table)
availability and licence: public on IEEE DataPort; licence not stated on the page read
known issues: container formats with embedded objects; random block sampling; a ceiling attributed to intrinsic ambiguity by two author groups
relevance to us: low — shows a benchmark whose ceiling is set by label ambiguity, and a possible fragment-level leak

name / short id: F04 VFF-16
reference: Described only through a user of the dataset: Liu et al., ByteNet, arXiv:2410.20855 <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.20855>; original reference not retrieved
size: 16 types; 1.6 M samples at 512 bytes, 209K at 4,096 bytes (secondary)
label source and quality: source-file type (secondary)
tools evaluated and headline results: ByteFormer 78.8% (4,096 bytes) and 78.1% (512 bytes)
known issues: known only through a citing paper
relevance to us: low — completeness

name / short id: F05 NapierOne
reference: Davies, Macfarlane, Buchanan, "NapierOne: A modern mixed file data set alternative to Govdocs1", Forensic Science International: Digital Investigation 40, 301330 (2022), DOI 10.1016/j.fsidi.2021.301330; arXiv:2201.08154 <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.08154>. Data: www.napierone.com and the AWS Open Data registry <https://registry.opendata.aws/napierone/>
size: nearly 500,000 unique files; 44 file types; typically 5,000 files per type
file source: gov.uk, CommonCrawl, Project Gutenberg, clean operating-system installs, AndroZoo, VirusTotal and others
file names available?: yes; the type is embedded in the file name
label source and quality: files checked for 'the correct magic numbers', 'verified to confirm that they could be opened successfully using the appropriate application', SHA1-deduplicated, virus-scanned
taxonomy: 44 types chosen by consensus of ten popularity lists; script classes: JavaScript, PowerShell, CSS, HTML
splits and leakage control: no predefined split (a corpus, not a task); no duplicates by SHA1
tools evaluated and headline results: none in the paper
known issues: few code classes
relevance to us: low — the best example of label validation by independent means in this neighbouring field

name / short id: F06 RealDC subset of Sester et al.
reference: Sester, Hayes, Scanlon, Le-Khac, "A comparative study of support vector machine and neural networks for file type identification using n-gram analysis", FSI: Digital Investigation 36, 301121, 2021, DOI 10.1016/j.fsidi.2021.301121, proof PDF <https://activityinsight.pace.edu/dhayes/intellcont/FSIDI301121_proof-1.pdf>
granularity: file (5,000 bytes after removing the first 200)
size: 12,000 files; 6 types
label source and quality: types pre-sorted with the corpus
taxonomy: xls, doc, csv, txt, jpg, ppt
splits and leakage control: 1,000 train and 1,000 test files per type
tools evaluated and headline results: linear SVM 91.49% (unigrams); neural networks 85.8% to 85.9%; a literature table of 17 studies with accuracies from 27.5% to 99.5% on incomparable datasets
known issues: six types
relevance to us: low — documents incomparability across private corpora

name / short id: F07 Koch-2022 polyglot set (generated with mitra)
reference: Koch, Oesch, Chaulagain, Adkisson, Erwin, Weber, "Toward the Detection of Polyglot Files", CSET 2022, pp. 120-128, DOI 10.1145/3546096.3546106; arXiv:2203.07561, read at ar5iv <https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2203.07561>
size: 31,199 training and 7,799 test monoglots (7 types); 25,210 training and 6,303 test polyglots (21 combinations)
label source and quality: known by construction
tools evaluated and headline results: the file utility detects 28.11% of polyglots (2.56% for appended 'stack' polyglots); best models about 95% recall
known issues: synthetic; detectors may learn generator artefacts
relevance to us: low — shows that single-label ground truth is a modelling choice

name / short id: F08 Koch-2025 polyglot set (generated with Fazah)
reference: Koch et al., "On the Abuse and Detection of Polyglot Files", WWW 2025, DOI 10.1145/3696410.3714814; arXiv PDF titled 'Where the Polyglots Are ...', arXiv:2407.01529 <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.01529>
size: test: 9,975 monoglots and 213,109 polyglots; 46 format combinations; plus 30 in-the-wild samples from 15 attack chains
file source: benign files collected via the GitHub API, combined by the Fazah generator
label source and quality: known by construction; multi-label
taxonomy: multi-label; covert formats include HTA, PHP, JavaScript, PowerShell
splits and leakage control: donor files segregated between training and test
tools evaluated and headline results: PolyConv: F1 99.20% for polyglot detection, 99.47% for multi-label format identification; polyfile about 93.32% and polydet about 83.74% (existing-tool numbers to check); Magika not evaluated
known issues: synthetic apart from 30 real samples
relevance to us: low — precedent for splitting by source object and for multi-label truth

name / short id: F09 IDCC16 Purdue format-identification comparison (id invented)
reference: Kumaravel, Dearborn, Witt, Kuang, "Measuring the Accuracy of File Format Identification Tools", IDCC 2016 poster: PDF <https://dcc.ac.uk/sites/default/files/documents/IDCC16/76_measuringAccuracyFileFormatIdentificationTools_web.pdf>. Grey literature
size: about 16,232 files
file source: not described in the poster text read
label source and quality: none independent: the poster reports inter-tool agreement; ground-truth method not described
tools evaluated and headline results: DROID, FIDO, Siegfried: 14,552 files (89.65%) identified identically by all
known issues: agreement instead of accuracy
relevance to us: low — shows the fallback when there is no independent truth

name / short id: F10 UK Web Domain Dataset format study (Jackson 2012)
reference: Jackson, "Formats over Time: Exploring UK Web History", arXiv:1210.1714 <https://arxiv.org/pdf/1210.1714>
size: 2.5 billion resources (35 TB compressed), 1996-2010
label source and quality: none independent: server MIME type, DROID (binary signatures) and Apache Tika compared
tools evaluated and headline results: Tika failed to identify about 1% of resources, DROID about 10%; weak signature matching for 'text-based formats like CSS, JavaScript, and older or malformed HTML'
known issues: no ground truth
relevance to us: low — signature tools are structurally weak on text formats

name / short id: F11 MITRE 2009 file-format identification study
reference: Vidrine, "File Format Identification: Report on MITRE Sponsored Research", MITRE technical report 10-0004: PDF <https://www.mitre.org/sites/default/files/pdf/10_0004.pdf>. Grey literature
size: corpus not described in the text read
label source and quality: ground-truth procedure not described
taxonomy: file formats; token-based validation proposed for source code such as Java and Perl
tools evaluated and headline results: file/libmagic about 80% accuracy; Oracle Outside In few errors but about 60% identification rate; DROID, TrID, mime-util none above 80%
known issues: undocumented corpus
relevance to us: low — separates identification rate (coverage) from accuracy

name / short id: F12 Apache Tika regression corpus
reference: Apache Tika wiki page on the regression corpus <https://cwiki-test.apache.org/confluence/x/2iKGBg>; Tika govdocs1 mirror README <https://corpora.tika.apache.org/base/docs/govdocs1/README.html>. Grey literature
size: 'below 1 TB and on the order of a few million files'
file source: Common Crawl CC-MAIN-2018-39 (earlier iterations included govdocs1)
label source and quality: selection by the 'detected mime' field that Common Crawl computes with Tika itself
"not code" / "other" labels?: 'a fairly large portion of octet-stream' kept on purpose
sampling: three-pass sampling by detected type; deliberate oversampling of non-ASCII and charset-less files
tools evaluated and headline results: Tika versions compared with each other (tika-eval); no accuracy against ground truth
known issues: tool-conditioned sampling
relevance to us: low — the file-type analogue of sampling a PLI corpus 'by Linguist language'
